questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT part of the current account?
options: Foreign direct investment inflows
Trade in goods
Primary income
Secondary income
questions.why: FDI is a financial account flow. The profits it later generates appear as primary income.
whyNot: Trade in goods is the first component.
Primary income covers profit, interest and wages from abroad.
Secondary income covers aid and remittances.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines primary income?
options: Income flows from investments and employment abroad: profit, interest, dividends and wages
Transfers with nothing given in return, such as aid
The value of exports of goods
Investment in productive assets abroad
questions.why: Repatriated profits of foreign-owned firms are a debit here, which is why FDI has a permanent negative effect on this line.
whyNot: That is secondary income.
That is trade in goods.
That is FDI, a financial account flow.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines secondary income?
options: Transfers with nothing given in return, chiefly aid and workers' remittances
Profit and interest earned abroad
Trade in services
Changes in official reserves
questions.why: Remittances are a major credit for several developing economies.
whyNot: That is primary income.
That is part of the trade balance.
That is a financial account item.

questions.stem: What is the balance of trade?
options: Exports of goods and services minus imports of goods and services
The current account balance
Exports of goods minus imports of goods only
The sum of the current and financial accounts
questions.why: The current account is the balance of trade plus the two income balances.
whyNot: The current account also includes income flows.
The balance of trade covers services as well as goods.
That must sum to zero.

questions.stem: Exports of goods 118, imports 156, exports of services 64, imports 41. What is the balance of trade?
options: A deficit of 15
A deficit of 38
A surplus of 23
A deficit of 53
whyNot: That is the goods balance alone.
That is the services balance alone.
That adds the two deficits incorrectly.

questions.stem: Balance of trade -15, primary income -14, secondary income +9. What is the current account balance?
options: A deficit of 20
A deficit of 38
A surplus of 20
A deficit of 29
whyNot: That omits the income balances.
The components sum to a negative figure.
That omits the secondary income credit.

questions.stem: A current account deficit is $20bn and GDP is $420bn. What is the deficit as a share of GDP?
questions.why: (20 / 420) x 100 = 4.8%. This is the standard way to judge whether a deficit is large.
whyNot: That inverts the calculation.
That misplaces the decimal point.
That uses an incorrect calculation.

questions.stem: Why must the balance of payments accounts sum to zero?
options: A current account deficit must be paid for by selling assets or borrowing, which are financial account credits
Governments adjust the figures to make them balance
Exports always equal imports over time
The capital account offsets the financial account exactly
questions.why: The deficit is necessarily matched by a financial account surplus, which is an inflow of investment or borrowing.
whyNot: It follows from the accounting, not from adjustment.
Trade can be persistently imbalanced.
The capital account is small and does not perform this role.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a cause of a current account deficit?
options: Poor international competitiveness from low productivity and high unit labour costs
A weak exchange rate combined with high productivity
High domestic saving relative to investment
Large income inflows from investments held abroad
questions.why: A strong currency, high domestic demand and low saving relative to investment are the other main causes.
whyNot: That combination tends to produce a surplus.
High saving relative to investment produces a surplus.
Income inflows are a current account credit.

questions.stem: Why is how a deficit is financed more important than its size?
options: Long-term FDI into productive capacity is sustainable, while short-term borrowing can reverse suddenly
The size of a deficit cannot be measured accurately
Financing has no effect on the exchange rate
All financing sources carry identical risk
questions.why: A sudden reversal of hot money forces a sharp depreciation and a contraction, whereas FDI cannot leave overnight.
whyNot: It is measured routinely.
A reversal of financing moves the exchange rate sharply.
FDI and short-term flows differ greatly in mobility.

questions.stem: The current account balance equals which of the following?
options: National saving minus investment
National saving plus investment
Government spending minus taxation
Exports minus government borrowing
questions.why: A country investing more than it saves must import capital, which appears as a current account deficit. This is the most analytically powerful way to express it.
whyNot: It is the difference, not the sum.
That is the fiscal balance.
That is not an identity.

questions.stem: Why is an expenditure reducing policy criticised as a way of correcting a deficit?
options: It reduces output and employment as well as imports, and does nothing about competitiveness
It has no effect on import spending
It raises the exchange rate automatically
It is prohibited by the IMF
questions.why: The improvement lasts only while demand is suppressed, so the account improves at the cost of a recession.
whyNot: Lower total demand reduces import spending directly.
Tighter policy may raise the rate, but that is not the criticism.
The IMF has historically recommended it.

questions.stem: Why is supply-side policy described as the only permanent solution to a deficit?
options: It raises competitiveness, so exports rise for structural reasons rather than through suppressed demand
It works faster than any other policy
It requires no government spending
It removes the need for imports
questions.why: It addresses the root cause and raises output rather than reducing it, and it works over years rather than months.
whyNot: It is the slowest of the three approaches.
Education and infrastructure are expensive.
Imports of inputs continue and may rise.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an expenditure switching policy?
options: A depreciation of the currency
Higher interest rates
Higher income tax
Investment in education and training
questions.why: Switching policies shift spending from imports to domestic goods; tariffs and quotas are the other examples.
whyNot: That is expenditure reducing.
That is expenditure reducing.
That is supply-side.

questions.stem: Why are large global trade imbalances regarded as significant?
options: The financial flows recycling surpluses into deficit countries can encourage excessive borrowing
They always cause exchange rates to be fixed
They prevent countries from trading with each other
They have no macroeconomic consequences
questions.why: They also build up external liabilities, create political pressure for protection, and make sudden adjustment disruptive.
whyNot: They create pressure on floating rates rather than fixing them.
Trade continues; the concern is its financing.
They contributed to the conditions before 2008.

questions.stem: When are trade imbalances least likely to be a problem?
options: When they reflect genuine differences in demographics, development stage and investment opportunities
When they are very large as a share of GDP
When they are financed by short-term capital inflows
When they persist for many years
questions.why: A young, fast-growing economy importing capital to build infrastructure should run a deficit.
whyNot: Size raises rather than reduces the concern.
Short-term financing makes a deficit fragile.
Persistence builds up external liabilities.
